rows.stem: Which of the following is not correct for \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) reaction ?

options.label: C
options.text: Proceeds through the formation of carbocation

rows.solution:
Three of the four statements are hallmarks of \(\mathrm{S_N}1\). The rate depends only on the substrate, since the slow step is the ionisation of the substrate alone, so the kinetics are first order. A polar protic solvent helps, because it stabilises both the carbocation and the departing anion. And the route goes through a carbocation intermediate by definition.

What \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) does NOT give is inversion of configuration. The carbocation is planar, so the nucleophile attacks equally from either face and the product is a racemic mixture. Clean inversion is the signature of \(\mathrm{S_N}2\), where the nucleophile must attack from the side opposite the leaving group. So the statement about inversion is the one that is not correct.

rows.stem: Dehydration of tertiary alcohols with Cu at 573 K gives :
rows.solution:
Copper at 573 K acts differently on the three classes of alcohol, and the difference is diagnostic. A primary alcohol is dehydrogenated to an aldehyde and a secondary alcohol to a ketone — in both cases a hydrogen is available on the carbon bearing the \(-\mathrm{OH}\). A tertiary alcohol has no such hydrogen, so dehydrogenation is impossible; instead it undergoes DEHYDRATION, losing water to give an alkene:
\(\mathrm{R_3C-OH} \xrightarrow[573\ \mathrm{K}]{\mathrm{Cu}} \text{alkene} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)

rows.subtopic: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds
rows.stem: The coordination number of Co in \(\mathrm{[Co(en)_2Cl_2]^{+}}\) is :
rows.solution:
The coordination number is the number of ligand donor ATOMS bonded directly to the metal. Ethane-1,2-diamine is bidentate, donating through both of its nitrogen atoms, so two of them supply four donor atoms; the two chlorido ligands supply one each. That makes six, so the coordination number of cobalt is 6 and the complex is octahedral.

Counting ligand molecules instead — two en plus two chloride — gives 4, which is the distractor.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem: Which of the following transition metals shows +1 and +2 oxidation states ?
rows.solution:
Copper shows both \(+1\) and \(+2\). Its configuration is \([\mathrm{Ar}]\,3d^{10} 4s^1\): losing the single \(4s\) electron gives \(\mathrm{Cu^{+}}\), \(3d^{10}\), and losing one more from the d subshell gives \(\mathrm{Cu^{2+}}\), \(3d^9\). Both cuprous and cupric compounds are common.

Zinc shows only \(+2\); iron shows \(+2\) and \(+3\); chromium shows \(+2\), \(+3\) and \(+6\) — none of the three has a common \(+1\) state.

rows.stem: The correct order of decreasing order of \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) values is :
rows.solution:
A HIGHER \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) means a WEAKER base, so putting the values in decreasing order means listing the weakest base first.

Ethylamine is much the strongest of the three: its nitrogen is attached only to an alkyl group, which pushes electron density towards the lone pair, so its \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) is lowest and it goes last. The other two have nitrogen attached directly to a benzene ring, which delocalises the lone pair and weakens them both sharply; between them, N-methylaniline has an extra methyl group donating electron density, so it is the stronger of the pair and aniline the weaker.

Decreasing \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) is therefore
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} > \mathrm{C_6H_5NHCH_3} > \mathrm{C_2H_5NH_2}\)
Reading the question as asking for decreasing BASIC strength would reverse the whole list, which is what the other options offer.

rows.stem: Each polypeptide in a protein has amino acids linked with each other in a specific sequence and it is this sequence of amino acids that is said to be :
rows.solution:
The primary structure of a protein is the sequence in which its amino acid residues are joined along the chain. Change one residue in that sequence and the protein becomes a different protein, which is why the primary structure is the most fundamental level.

The secondary structure is how the chain folds locally into an \(\alpha\)-helix or a \(\beta\)-pleated sheet; the tertiary structure is the overall three-dimensional shape of the chain; and the quaternary structure describes how several separate chains assemble, as the four subunits of haemoglobin do.

rows.stem: Benzene diazonium chloride on reaction with phenol in weakly basic medium gives :
rows.solution:
This is azo coupling. In weakly basic medium phenol is partly converted to the even more strongly activated phenoxide ion, and the benzenediazonium ion acts as a weak electrophile attacking the position para to the \(-\mathrm{OH}\):
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^-} + \mathrm{C_6H_5OH} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{OH^-}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-N{=}N-C_6H_4-OH\ (p)} + \mathrm{HCl}\)
The product is p-hydroxyazobenzene, an orange dye. Note the diazonium group is KEPT here rather than replaced, which is what distinguishes a coupling from all the Sandmeyer-type reactions.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3\,C - O - CH_3}\) gives \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3\,C - I}\) and \(\mathrm{CH_3OH}\) on reaction with HI.
Reason (R) : The reaction occurs by \(\mathrm{S_N1}\) mechanism.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
The products named in the Assertion are the right ones. When \((\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C-O-CH_3}\) is protonated and then cleaved, the \(\mathrm{C-O}\) bond that breaks is the one to the TERTIARY carbon, because that carbon can support a relatively stable carbocation. The iodide ion then captures it, and the methyl group leaves with the oxygen as methanol:
\((\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C-O-CH_3} + \mathrm{HI} \longrightarrow (\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{C-I} + \mathrm{CH_3OH}\)

The Reason gives exactly the mechanism responsible: the reaction goes by \(\mathrm{S_N}1\) precisely because a tertiary carbocation is accessible, and it is that route which decides which fragment gets the iodine. Had both groups been primary, the mechanism would have been \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) and the iodide would have attacked the less hindered carbon instead. So the Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Diazonium salts of aromatic amines are less stable than those of aliphatic amines.
Reason (R) : Diazonium salts of aromatic amines undergo resonance.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Aromatic diazonium salts are MORE stable than aliphatic ones, not less — stable enough to be isolated at low temperature, while aliphatic ones decompose the instant they form. So the Assertion is false.

The Reason is true, and it is in fact the reason the Assertion is false: resonance delocalises the positive charge of an aryl diazonium ion into the benzene ring, and that is precisely what stabilises it. So the Assertion is false while the Reason is true.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : For complex reaction, order of reaction is given by the slowest step.
Reason (R) : Order of reaction is not applicable for the complex reaction.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
For a complex reaction the observed order is set by the slowest step, the rate-determining step, so the Assertion is true.

The Reason contradicts it. Order IS applicable to complex reactions — indeed the Assertion has just described how it is obtained for one. It is MOLECULARITY that has no meaning for a complex reaction, since it counts the species colliding in a single elementary step. So the Assertion is true while the Reason is false.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : \(\mathrm{E^{o}_{Mn^{2+}/Mn}}\) value is highly negative.
Reason (R) : Because \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\) is highly stable due to half-filled \(\mathrm{3d^5}\) configuration.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below.

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution: The standard electrode potential of the manganese couple is unusually negative, so the Assertion is true, and the Reason names the cause. Removing two electrons from a manganese atom leaves \(\mathrm{Mn^{2+}}\), which is \(3d^5\) — an exactly half-filled subshell with all five spins parallel, and therefore especially stable. Because the product ion is so favourable, the metal gives up those electrons readily, the oxidation is strongly favoured, and the reduction potential is correspondingly low. The Reason is the correct explanation of the Assertion.

rows.stem:
Write IUPAC names of the following compounds :
(a) \(\mathrm{[Ag(NH_3)_2]\,[Ag(CN)_2]}\)
(b) \(\mathrm{[Co(en)_3]_2\,(SO_4)_3}\)
rows.solution:
(a) The compound is made of a complex cation and a complex anion, and the cation is named first. Silver is \(+1\) in each: in \(\mathrm{[Ag(NH_3)_2]^+}\) the two ammine ligands are neutral, and in \(\mathrm{[Ag(CN)_2]^-}\) two cyanido ligands at \(-1\) each leave the metal at \(+1\) against an overall \(-1\). An anionic complex takes the Latin stem with the \(-ate\) ending, so silver becomes argentate. The name is diamminesilver(I) dicyanidoargentate(I).

(b) Three sulphate ions contribute \(-6\), so the two complex cations carry \(+3\) each. Ethane-1,2-diamine is neutral, so the whole \(+3\) belongs to the metal. Because the ligand's own name contains numerals the multiplying prefix is tris rather than tri. The name is tris(ethane-1,2-diamine)cobalt(III) sulphate.

rows.stem: What is the effect of denaturation on the structure of proteins ? What are the common types of secondary structures of proteins ?
rows.solution:
Denaturation destroys the SECONDARY and TERTIARY structure of a protein while leaving the PRIMARY structure intact. Heat, or a change in pH, disturbs the hydrogen bonds and other weak interactions that hold the chain in its folded shape, so the helix uncoils and the globule unfolds. The peptide bonds themselves are not broken, so the sequence of amino acid residues survives — but the protein loses its biological activity, because that activity depends on the shape and not on the sequence alone. Coagulating the white of an egg is the everyday example.

The common types of secondary structure are the \(\alpha\)-helix and the \(\beta\)-pleated sheet.

rows.stem:
Draw the structures of major products in each of the following reactions :
(a) \(\mathrm{(CH_3)_3\,CBr + KOH} \xrightarrow[\mathrm{Heat}]{\mathrm{Ethanol}}\)
(b) 4-nitrocumene \(\mathrm{+\ Br_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{Heat}}\)
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — part (b)'s substrate is printed as a SKELETAL DRAWING: a benzene ring carrying \(\mathrm{CH(CH_3)_2}\) at one vertex and \(\mathrm{O_2N}\) at the vertex three bonds round, i.e. PARA (vertices traced individually at 3x). It is NAMED losslessly in the stem as 4-nitrocumene, so the row is answerable from text alone; naming a REACTANT cannot state the answer, because the question asks for the PRODUCT. The reading is independently confirmed by the marking scheme, whose answer for (b) is drawn as the same ring bearing \(\mathrm{O_2N}\) and \(\mathrm{C(Br)(CH_3)_2}\). Page idx 10.
rows.solution:
(a) Potassium hydroxide in ETHANOL, with heat, acts as a base rather than a nucleophile, so the reaction is elimination. A \(\beta\) hydrogen is removed together with the bromide and a double bond forms:
\((\mathrm{CH_3})_3\mathrm{CBr} + \mathrm{KOH\ (alc.)} \xrightarrow{\Delta} (\mathrm{CH_3})_2\mathrm{C{=}CH_2} + \mathrm{KBr} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)
The major product is 2-methylpropene. Aqueous potassium hydroxide would have substituted instead, giving the tertiary alcohol.

(b) Bromine with heat attacks the side chain rather than the ring, and within the side chain it takes the BENZYLIC hydrogen, whose radical is stabilised by the ring. In 4-nitrocumene that hydrogen sits on the tertiary carbon of the isopropyl group — benzylic and tertiary at once:
\(\mathrm{4\text{-}O_2N{-}C_6H_4{-}CH(CH_3)_2} + \mathrm{Br_2} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{4\text{-}O_2N{-}C_6H_4{-}CBr(CH_3)_2} + \mathrm{HBr}\)
The major product is 2-bromo-2-(4-nitrophenyl)propane. The nitro group deactivates the ring, which makes side-chain attack the more favourable route still.

rows.stem:
Gives the structures of A, B and C in the following reactions :
(a) 4-nitrotoluene \(\xrightarrow{\mathrm{Fe + HCl}}\) A \(\xrightarrow[0 - 5\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}]{\mathrm{NaNO_2 + HCl}}\) B \(\xrightarrow{\mathrm{H_2O}}\) C
(b) benzenediazonium chloride \(\xrightarrow{\mathrm{CuCN}}\) A \(\xrightarrow[\text{Partial hydrolysis}]{\mathrm{OH^{-}}}\) B \(\xrightarrow{\mathrm{NaOBr}}\) C
rows.figureNote: ILLUSTRATIVE — both substrates are printed as SKELETAL DRAWINGS: (a) a benzene ring carrying \(\mathrm{NO_2}\) at the top vertex and \(\mathrm{CH_3}\) at the vertex directly opposite (para), and (b) a benzene ring carrying \(\mathrm{N_2^{+}\,Cl^{-}}\). Both are NAMED losslessly in the stem, so the row is answerable from text alone; naming a REACTANT cannot state the answer, because the question asks for the PRODUCTS A, B and C. Both readings are independently confirmed by the marking scheme's worked answer (A for (a) is p-toluidine and C is p-cresol; A for (b) is benzonitrile). Page idx 10.
rows.solution:
(a) Iron with hydrochloric acid reduces the nitro group to an amino group and leaves the methyl group alone:
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{4\text{-}H_3C{-}C_6H_4{-}NH_2}\), 4-methylaniline
Sodium nitrite in hydrochloric acid at \(0-5\ ^{\circ}\mathrm{C}\) diazotises that amine:
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{4\text{-}H_3C{-}C_6H_4{-}N_2^+Cl^-}\), 4-methylbenzenediazonium chloride
Warming with water replaces the diazonium group by a hydroxyl group, nitrogen leaving as gas:
\(\mathrm{C} = \mathrm{4\text{-}H_3C{-}C_6H_4{-}OH}\), 4-methylphenol

(b) Cuprous cyanide replaces the diazonium group by cyanide — the Sandmeyer reaction:
\(\mathrm{A} = \mathrm{C_6H_5CN}\), benzonitrile
PARTIAL hydrolysis stops at the amide rather than going on to the acid, which is what the word partial is doing in the question:
\(\mathrm{B} = \mathrm{C_6H_5CONH_2}\), benzamide
Sodium hypobromite brings about the Hofmann bromamide degradation, removing the carbonyl carbon and leaving a primary amine with one carbon fewer:
\(\mathrm{C} = \mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2}\), aniline
The sequence has come full circle: the benzenediazonium chloride was itself made from aniline, and three steps later the aniline is back with the same number of ring carbons.
